newsitem.title: UK: Euro Products Outlook - Fuel softer, rest steady.
newsitem.headline: Euro Products Outlook - Fuel softer, rest steady.

text.p: European high sulphur fuel oil prices are poised to slip this week on rising supplies but the outlook for other products is for a sideways summer drift awaiting fresh news of Iraqi crude exports, traders said.

High sulphur cracked fuel is likely to soften in northwest Europe with the appearance late last week of fresh Russian cargoes. One regular buyer spoke of 120,000 tonnes loading in Klaipeda and St Petersburg by August 4.
But the Mediterranean is seen tight after excess supply has been siphoned off by demand into Portugal, Tunisia and Greece.

Supply of low sulphur cracked fuel is healthy in NWE and with an anticipated lull in demand from Italy and a notionally closed transatlantic arbitrage,this is expected to prevent rises far above the $95 fob NWE paid at the end of the week.
Straight-run is tight in both regions, and expensive. A spate of deals last week at around $106-$108 fob NWE cleared out most of the early-August supply of low sulphur North Sea cargoes.
Russian high sulphur exports have been limited. This has pushed premiums up to $6 or $7 over the mean/mean of quotes for M-100 material, while E-4 has soared to mean/mean/mean +$7-$8.
The outlook for gas oil is less clear in the absence of steady trade, with most players saying spreads are likely to bump along at current depressed levels.

The heating oil/low sulphur diesel spread is seen continuing at around $4 or $5, depressed by low demand and high European distillate stocks. The exception appears to be EN590, which is enjoying modest demand into Le Havre, Rostock and Hamburg.
Cargo differentials of August IPE +$1 for heating oil and +$4.50 for low sulphur diesel and barge differentials of screen plus 25/50 cents are unlikely to change greatly.

Barge demand has been stalled by dollar strength against the mark, which has made gas oil expensive into Germany, and by active buying seen in June. But buyers are likely to return if a return of Iraqi oil makes outright values more atrractive.
Gasoline is set to remain tight and prices broadly stable at least through next week, and possibly until mid-August.

"Europe is fundamentally long, but it'll be just a matter of one or two weeks before price levels start coming off," said a U.S. refiner. "Around mid-August we'll probably see the arb to the U.S. opening due to expected weakening in Europe."
A German barge player said the gasoline market currently looked strong, "but at the same time it's very U.S.-led, so we'll have to wait and see what the U.S. does."
Naphtha should remain steady or strengthen slightly with the market broadly balanced between reluctant buyers and lack of available volumes.
"It'll be up a tad," a U.K. trader said. "There's not a lot of material around in NWE and buyers will have to come out of the woodwork sooner or later."
Large cargo availabilities are expected to remain scarce.
Most Med volumes are committed to Asia after a recent wave of arb-related flows. Smaller sized ARA cargoes will remain more plentiful in the light of high refinery production of naphtha, traders say.
